note_tweet.text:
What does poverty look like beyond income?

Someone can live above an income poverty line and still go without electricity, clean drinking water, or schooling.

The global Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI), from the Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative and the UN Development Programme, counts the deprivations people face at the same time. We recently updated our 16 charts with the 2026 release, published in October, which adds new surveys for 13 countries.

The MPI looks at ten indicators in three areas, using data from household surveys: health (nutrition and child mortality), education (years of schooling and school attendance), and living standards (cooking fuel, sanitation, drinking water, electricity, housing, and assets). People deprived in a third or more of the weighted indicators count as “multidimensionally poor”. You can read more about how the MPI works in our article.

The chart shows this for Nigeria, which has a new survey from 2024. About half of Nigerians live in a household without electricity, about half in one without adequate sanitation, and more than three-quarters in one that cooks with solid fuels like wood or charcoal. 12% live in a household where a child has died in the previous five years.

(This data update was led by @parriagadap.)

note_tweet.text:
Anthropic is about to sell the public a trillion-dollar company controlled by 2 shares worth less than a penny.

And the people buying it will have almost no way to change anything that happens next.

I read the voting section of Anthropic's IPO filing, and I think it's the most one-sided deal ever offered to regular investors at this size:

There is exactly ONE Class F share. It belongs to an LLC owned by 7 of Anthropic's co-founders, and it carries 50.1% of all the votes.

There is exactly ONE Class T share. It belongs to Anthropic's Long-Term Benefit Trust, and it elects a majority of the board.

If Anthropic were ever liquidated, each of those 2 shares would get its par value of $0.00001.

The public gets Class A shares instead. And Anthropic's own filing says this structure may effectively eliminate their ability to influence important decisions, including a sale of the company.

So here's what that means for anyone who buys:

- They can't replace the board if the company stumbles, because the trust picks the majority and the founders hold half the vote.
- They can't push for a sale, even if someone offers a huge premium.
- They can't stop the board from putting the mission ahead of their money. Anthropic is a public benefit corporation, so the board has to weigh shareholders against the long-term benefit of humanity.
- And they can't easily sue over it. Delaware law requires at least 2% of the shares or $2 million worth of stock to bring that kind of claim.

This isn't some far-off hypothetical either.

The filing warns that slowing AI development for safety may not maximize stockholder value. It also says Anthropic recently paused training a next-generation model for more than a month over safety and security concerns.

A public shareholder would've had zero say in that pause.

And here's the part I can't get past:

Each co-founder has pledged to give 80% of their Anthropic equity to charity. The Class F vote stays at 50.1% no matter how much stock they still own.

So the founders can give away most of their money and keep all of their control.

Dario Amodei told 60 Minutes last year that he's deeply uncomfortable with AI decisions being made by a few companies and a few people. When he was asked who elected him, he said no one.

Now his company's IPO hands 50.1% of the votes to 7 people, and he's one of them.

And guess who's being lined up to buy it?

Anthropic has weighed reserving 15% to 20% of the IPO for individual investors, according to Bloomberg. JPMorgan is leading the US retail push, and Citigroup is handling retail buyers in places like Japan, Britain and Canada.

The same filing warns that AI could pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.

So regular people are being asked to buy a company that says its product could threaten humanity, with no real vote on how it's run.

Anthropic's answer is that this is the whole point. The structure is built to keep Wall Street from pressuring it into cutting corners on safety. The trustees have no financial stake in the company. Google and Meta gave their founders control and still made shareholders rich. And every buyer gets all of this in writing before they buy.

But Zuckerberg's control comes from shares he owns, so when Meta's stock falls, he loses money too. Anthropic's 2 control shares can't lose anything.

Anyone buying this IPO is paying full price to hand control to 7 founders and 5 trustees.

They're desperate for money and they don't care about your money.

Apparently everyone in Renaissance Florence was accusing each other of being gay all the time.

Between 1432 and 1502, this city of 40,000 persons would investigate 17,000 men for homosexuality, meaning that half or more of all men would be investigated during their life.

Since you could report anyone anonymously to the authorities by dropping a note, and the punishments for those convicted were financial fines and political disbarment, there was both a low bar and financial incentives to investigate people, plus benefits if financial or political rivals were accused.

Leonardo da Vinci was accused anonymously twice, probably due to his association with the Medici, and although cleared, bitterly complained about the Florentine justice system in his notes afterwards.

note_tweet.text:
Couple thoughts:

1) After several people pointed out that Lyman couldn't substitute all-cause mortality for malaria-specific mortality like he had done, he fixed it. His initial estimate for $/lives saved was $19000; revised it’s about $8,200. 

2) I think, though I could be wrong about this, that his calculation to get $8200 still has a problem: he calculates the costs of the distribution based on the whole population but the benefits based on 75% of the population (since he argues the other 25% is already sleeping under nets). But as he himself identifies, the nice thing about an intention-to-treat analysis is that you don't need to do this and shouldn't: you just ask how much to expect mortality to fall in a village after handing out the nets, and the answer is 17%. (You only care about the fact some people are already sleeping under nets if that makes your village unlike the one where the  17% was measured; more on that below.) If he changed this one factor this would make his numbers quite close to GiveWell's.

3) He then applies an adjustment for the long-term: "If bednets reduced short-run all-cause mortality by 18% in the 1990s and maybe reduce it by (who knows?) 14% today, they probably reduce actual child mortality (i.e. across 5 years of early childhood) by 7-11%." 

But GiveWell actually accounts for that even more stringently by just excluding all benefits past the first two years, one of several places where they are intentionally conservative. 

4) He accuses GiveWell of misrepresenting Cochrane's statistics  but they actually just report a bunch of different numbers and I think he mixed them up. He complains "GiveWell cites that review to support a “45% reduction in malaria incidence.” That’s an error, that review did not find a 45% reduction in malaria incidence." But the review absolutely does report almost exactly that: "Insecticide-treated nets also reduce the incidence of uncomplicated episodes of Plasmodium falciparum malaria by almost a half (rate ratio 0.55, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.64; 5 trials, 35,551 participants, high-certainty evidence". Rate ratio 0.55 means a 45% reduction. 

5) He expresses concern that a lot of the Cochrane studies are old and describe a different environment (Africa in the late 1990s/early 2000s). However, GiveWell's most recent grant to nets in the DRC - which I believe that my donations helped to fund - is based on data from a 2023-2024 large scale demographic survey in the DRC, so the nets are being distributed in an environment very close to the one studied. It found about a 14% all-cause mortality reduction in the first year after a distribution, close to the 17% in Cochrane. 

He also expresses concern that Cochrane's mortality estimate here is low-powered but I don't think it is (the analysis says "rate ratio 0.83, 95% CI 0.77 to 0.89; 5 trials, 200,833 participants, high-certainty evidence") so it's between 11% and 23% with a 95% CI!

6) He also raises questions about whether there are more people trying to hand out nets than nets to be handed out. GiveWell looked into that and determined that in the DRC, there was not enough funding to do all the distributions that were indicated, in part because the Global Fund caps how much it'll spend in any one country. 

7) Finally, he argues we should instead - from an altruistic perspective - spend our money however maximizes GDP. But I think there's a serious case that health interventions like combatting malaria are necessary for GDP growth to take off in DRC, just like the American South was kind of a backwater until we eradicated malaria there. Being constantly sick is horrible for productivity. Being only able to hire employees who are constantly sick is horrible for a business environment. GiveWell estimates that a $1,000,000 donation increases adult income for 80,000 children by 0.6%, which means that much of their modelled benefit of malaria nets *is* their GDP effects.

My best guess is that if you were a hard-nosed GDP maxxer you'd invest a lot in reducing the disease burden in poor countries.  Or maybe you'd go all in on making AI happen as fast as possible, something I rarely see EAs criticized for failing to do. I would probably donate more money to making AI go well if I had more of an idea of how to do that and it wouldn't create a bunch of conflicts of interest with my reporting work.

I agree it would be cool if there were an organization focused on effective institutional capacity building in poor countries, but the reason I and man others don't donate to this is not that everyone fails to realize how important institutions are, it's that even though many people have worked very hard on the problem for a long time they do not have a way better than the nets to turn my money into GDP growth in poor countries. 

There was a bit of a Our World In Data article I read this fall that has stuck with me: 

"I’ve never had malaria, but I know several people who have. They describe it as one of the worst experiences of their life.

What starts out feeling like the flu — which is bad enough — can quickly progress into something far worse. The body swings from intense fever and sweats to chills deep enough to make you shake uncontrollably. Everything aches, from your muscles and joints to the pounding headache that makes it impossible to think clearly. Your body is so fatigued that it’s a battle to make it to the bathroom when the nausea and vomiting arrive.

That’s what a pretty standard infection feels like. For some, it goes much further. Here is how one account describes it:

“I awoke to what felt like lightning going through my legs, and then spreading through my body and in my head. Probably the worst headache, body aches, and chills you could possibly imagine. It felt like I was being stung repeatedly by an electric shock gun and could barely control my movements. The pain was so intense; I actually believed I was dying, literally crying out in pain so bad that I was taken to a 24-hour clinic that night at 3am.”

In Senegal, the median child experienced 43 attacks of malaria over the course of their childhood. My hard-nosed productivity obsessed persona says "I bet that's rough on their human capital development, and it's quite cheap to prevent." But mostly I don't, actually, say that to myself. I just buy some nets. If something even better comes along I'll do that, but I haven't seen it yet.
